newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenian rail workers stage four-hour strike.
newsitem.headline: Slovenian rail workers stage four-hour strike.

text.p: Thousands of Slovenian rail users had to find alternative means of transport on Tuesday morning as railway workers staged a four-hour strike demanding higher wages and holiday pay.

Olga Zvanut, spokeswoman for the state-owned railways, told Reuters all international trains, which are protected by Slovenian law, were running to schedule, as were all trains that began their journey before eight a.m. (0600 GMT).
"So far we have not recorded any major problems as most employees and students start work before eight a.m. (0600 GMT) when the strike started," she said.
The strike is the fourth by railway workers this year.
Railway employees said they would continue their industrial action if the government failed to meet their demands for a 14 percent increase in wages and a 70 percent rise in holiday pay.
"If no agreement is reached within a week, we will start a ten-day strike on May 20," Slavko Kmetic, head of the association of railway unions, told Reuters.
Currently the average gross salary of a railway worker is about 128,000 tolars ($828), well below the average Slovenian salary of 136,800 tolars.

Kmetic said the proposed strike would not affect international trains or those used by workers and students, but would affect most other passenger trains and nearly all cargo trains -- around 50 percent of all rail traffic.
"Negotiations so far have been entirely unsuccessful as the the management and the government insist on a mere three percent wage increase," he said.
Kmetic said the government had offered to increase holiday pay to 80,000 tolars from 74,000 tolars last year.

The government reiterated it could not agree to the demands because of the poor financial condition of the state-owned railways, which posted a loss of 3.6 billion tolars in 1996, down from a profit of 68 million in 1995.
The stoppages follow a series of strikes last year, which pushed the government into concessions prior to a general election in November.
